steps.text: Part 3 of 4: Loose pieces: what can be taken for free?. This part covers When it does not apply. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

A loose piece is free only if no defender can take back, and a defender can stand far away. A rook or queen guards along a whole file or row. A bishop or queen guards along a whole diagonal. A knight guards by its jump, a pawn the two squares diagonally ahead of it, and the king the squares beside it. Before you capture, trace lines back from the piece. Here is a defender that is easy to miss.

steps.caption: The bishop in the corner is far from the knight, but nothing stands between them on the long diagonal.

line.say: The rook takes the knight.
The bishop takes back from across the board. White lost a rook for a knight.

claims.statement: No black piece is loose.
The bishop on a8 defends the knight.
Taking the knight loses the rook for a knight.

steps.caption: A rook standing behind the piece guards it just as well. Here the rook on d8 defends the knight.

line.say: The rook takes the knight.
The other rook takes back along the file. Rook for knight.

claims.statement: The rook on d8 defends the knight.
Taking the knight loses a rook for a knight.

steps.text: A defender can also fail while it still stands there. Edward Lasker's *Chess Strategy* names three ways: a cheaper piece can capture the defender, a bigger threat elsewhere can pull it away, or it can be **pinned** (my paraphrase, from our reading notes). Look at a pinned one: it guards on paper but cannot take back.

steps.caption: Defended on paper. The bishop on e6 guards the knight, but the rook on e1 pins it to the king, so it cannot take back.

line.say: The rook takes the knight.
Black cannot recapture: the pinned bishop may not leave the e-file.

claims.statement: On paper the bishop on e6 defends the knight.
The rook still wins the knight.
Taking the knight is the engine's best move.

steps.text: The second question is what the capture costs. A piece that guards something important may be needed where it stands. Look at the first row of the next board: White's rook is the only piece keeping the king safe.

steps.title: Same attack, one change
steps.prompt: Predict first: does Black win a piece in each position?

steps.caption: The knight is loose, but White's king has no flight square: its own pawns block the second row.

line.say: The rook takes the knight and leaves the first row.
Black's rook lands on the first row. The king cannot move or capture: checkmate.

claims.statement: The knight on d5 is loose.
Taking the knight is a serious mistake.

steps.caption: The position after the capture, Black to move. One rook move ends the game.

line.say: The rook gives check on the first row. Nothing can block or capture, and the king has no square.

claims.statement: Re1 is checkmate.

steps.caption: With a pawn on h3, the king has the square h2. The rook can take the knight safely.

line.say: The rook takes the knight.
Black checks on the first row.
The king steps to h2, off the first row. The check is answered.

claims.statement: The rook wins the knight.
The king can step to h2.

steps.caption: Another duty. The rook on a3 is the only guard of the bishop on c3. The knight on a6 looks free, but the rook has a job.

line.say: The rook takes the knight and stops guarding the bishop.
The black bishop takes the bishop. The free knight was only an even trade.

claims.statement: The knight on a6 is loose.
Taking the knight is worse than the engine's best move.

steps.text: Two questions before every capture. **Is any piece defending it, even from far away, or only on paper?** **What does my capturing piece stop doing, and what is my opponent's most forcing reply: a check, a capture or a threat?** That scan has its own lesson in the loop course. If the answers are no and nothing, the piece really is free. Then a case where a defender exists, but the capture is still good.

steps.caption: The rook on d8 defends the knight, so it is not loose. But the capturer is only a pawn.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight.
The rook takes the pawn. White gave a pawn (1) for a knight (3).

claims.statement: The knight is not loose.
The rook on d8 defends the knight.
White comes out two points ahead.

steps.text: So **defended** means *not free*, but not always *safe to leave alone*: a cheap piece can attack an expensive defended one. Rule of thumb, from the counting values. A later lesson makes this exact by counting every attacker and defender. For now, one more fact. Attacking a loose piece does not win it if your opponent can move it.

steps.caption: Nothing is attacked yet. White attacks the knight, then it is Black's turn.

line.say: The rook attacks the knight, which is now loose. But it is Black's move.
The knight runs to a safe square. Nothing was won.

claims.statement: After the rook move the knight is loose.
Attacking the knight does not win it.

steps.caption: Often there is nothing to take. A common English-style move order, replayed with python-chess: after these six moves no piece on either side is loose.

line.say: White brings a knight out toward the centre.
Black mirrors with a knight.
A pawn grabs space and guards d5.
Black prepares to develop a bishop on the long diagonal.
A second knight comes out, defended by the b2 pawn.
The bishop takes the long diagonal.

claims.statement: No white piece is loose after six moves.
No black piece is loose after six moves.

steps.text: **Remember.** A loose piece is free only if nobody can take back, so trace lines from it for far-away defenders. A defender fails if it is pinned, and a capture can cost you if your capturing piece had another job. Ask: is any defender real, and what does my capturing piece stop doing? A cheap piece can even win a defended one.
